title: Brad Pitt’s new movie is a woke bait-and-switch | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

If “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” teaches us anything about the effortlessly cool fictional stuntman fromQuentin Tarantino’s 2019 movie “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood” (for whichBrad Pitt won an Oscar,essentially playing a version of himself), it’s not just that he’s macho. Or irresistible to women. Or that his butt looks good in bootcut jeans. It’s that he’s amensch.

This new movie, penned by Tarantino and directed this time around by David Fincher, takes place in the 1970s, but Cliff is a thoroughly modern man — perhaps evenpostmodern, given the caliber of some men these days. He takes loving care of his elderly father (and his father’s cat). He looks out for women and respects their boundaries and discretion, which seems to only make him more attractive to them. He’s a friend to the gay and Black communities. He’s considerate, dedicating songs on the radio to those he loves. And he lives by a strict moral code whereby he only metes out deadly violence when a transgressor wrongs someone with less power, including during his time fighting fascists in World War II. “I’m not that deep,” Cliff insists with a false modesty that is, once again, charming.

Cliff may still be a man — he doesn’t do enough laundry, plays tennis in outrageously inappropriate clothing and masturbates maybe a touch too much — but he’s also perhaps one of the best men we’ve seen on screen all year. As the film’staglinemakes clear, Cliff might be penniless and pitiless, but he’s also principled. In 2026, his version of masculinity feels like a miracle.

“Cliff Booth” arrives in theaters (and on Netflix next month) at an auspicious time. After the landslide wins for Democrats in the midterm elections, some liberals havejokingly declaredthe arrival of“Woke 3.0,”a political movement marked less by virtue signaling and more bycomically aggressive tolerance. Withyoung men shifting massivelyto the left, prognosticators have also begun writingobituaries for the misogynist manosphere. Amid this shift, the biggest entertainment release of the year — and potentially a generation — has been“Grand Theft Auto VI,”a revolutionary video game in which players must work to bea considerate boyfriend. Good men are back, it seems, even if they must occasionally kick butt when timing calls for it.

As chuds grapple with acultural realignmentin which theirtoxic version of masculinity seems to be against the ropes, “Cliff Booth”offers another surprisingly progressive male role model wrapped inside a bro-y“hangout movie.”Men who might be lured into the movie because of its cursory coolness and roster of big names —Tarantino,FincherandPittare all beloved (ifstillvaryinglyproblematic) figures for a very particular type of film bro — will reach its end credits having been both sated in their thirst for actionandgiven a commendable lesson in what it means to be a gentleman, albeit a deadly one. “Cliff Booth”may be a movie for dudes with a capital D, but it’s also, rather slyly, one of the wokest films of the year.

As the movie kicks off, it’s 1977 — eight years after the events of “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood” (roughly the same amount of time since the movie itself was released) — with the hippie counterculture having been replaced by Donna Summer and disco. Cliff is still legendary around town for having killed a bunch of Manson Family marauders (and thereby saving the life of Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate in this alternate universe), as well as once apparently beating up Bruce Lee, but the landscape has shifted. The audience is told Leonardo DiCaprio’s fading Western TV star Rick Dalton (who doesn’t appear in this film) has decamped to Australia, where he’s starring in a cheesy show that’s apparently a hit Down Under called “Dingo Dan.” (Robbie’s Tate, having survived the Manson Family killers in Tarantino’s alternate universe, does return for a brief cameo in a cigarette commercial.) With Rick having packed on too many pounds for his stunt double to continue to play him, Cliff has remained in Los Angeles, running a movie theater with the ease of a maestro conducting an orchestra, while also slinging fruity drinks at a tiki bar that boasts bikini mud-wrestling matches. Film work has mostly dried up, especially because Cliff’s joints seem creakier with age. “In Hollywood,” his father Gus (Peter Weller) explains to a customer at the pawn shop he runs, “two things matter: shelf life and shelf space.” Cliff seems to be running out of both.

Instead, he makes the most of his money as an under-the-table fixer for his old friends in the business, helping them when they get into trouble with nefarious figures. It’s during one of these quests that we’re reintroduced to Cliff as he works to protect a closeted gay director who’s been robbed and blackmailed by lowlifes. What irks Cliff most isn’t that the crooks robbed the director, but that they stole hisOscar. How could someone sink so low, he wants to know, genuinely confounded. Cliff’s justice is swift and deadly, but the quality of his mercy is not strained: although he kills a mobster, he’s open to giving a second chance to one of the other crooks,a young queer kid caught up in a bad crowd. Instead, Cliff drives him to a bus station and pays for his ticket home — with a stern warning that if he ever comes back to Los Angeles, Cliff won’t be so kind.

Eventually, a call from a no-nonsense but good-humored Australian agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), leads Cliff to Charlie Peters (Scott Caan, as this film’s stand-in for Dalton), an aging TV star with a Napoleon complex and a small problem with a pair of ruthless Filipino gangster brothers (JB Tadena and Matt Groove). They seem to be under the mistaken impression that Peters wanted them to kill his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), because he happened to get drunk one night in Manila and asked them to do just that. As Cliff works to untangle the mess, he and Karen also grow closer, mixing business and pleasure.

Despite this premise, “Cliff Booth” is actually rather light on plot. Tarantino’s script features some self-referential Easter eggs — at one point, two men dressed almost like John Travolta and Samuel L. Jackson in “Pulp Fiction”discuss Big Macs— but the film is, at its heart, a character study in which we’re invited to hang out with Cliff over the course of a week. It’s a slice-of-life movie, if the protagonist happened to also be one of the coolest people to have ever lived.

Cliff may be a male fantasy — or rather, an avatar for how many men wouldliketo fantasize about themselves. But “Cliff Booth” seems conscious of this pedestal, weaponizing it for the greater good of us all. Wanna spend time with Cliff? Or better yet, be like him? Etiquette school is in session.

As Peters says at one point as he introduces our hero to others on set, “Cliff Booth: the great white hope.”
